title: On Becoming a More Courageous Leader
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This post defines courageous leaders as people who feel the same fear as everyone else but act anyway. It challenges the view that courage is an innate trait, citing studies suggesting values matter more than family history. The central claim is that courage of conviction, a deep commitment to values or to people and outcomes, is what lets leaders face down fear. The practical move is to review core values, commit to them, and say them often with the team. Courage becomes learnable by becoming a more values-based person.
points: Courage is shown by action despite fear, not by the absence of fear.
Studies cited in the post link courageous behavior to personal values more than to family history or innate bravery.
Conviction about people or issues gives leaders the footing to stare down fear.
Reviewing core values and voicing them regularly with the team builds the courage needed in hard moments.
quotes: Courageous leaders have the same fears and trepidations as everyone else but make the choice to act anyway. We know a leader is courageous by what they do.
Yet, studies of leaders who consistently exhibit courage have revealed that values play a much more important role than any link to family history.
Leaders rally their ability to stare down their fear when they have a powerful conviction about the people or issues involved.
Leaders who know their values and stick to them regardless of the circumstances or social pressure are more likely to act courageously.
Leaders can learn to become more courageous by reviewing their core values and establishing a deep and abiding commitment to them.
Having courage doesn’t mean leaders run toward danger or relish trepidation. It means leaders don’t let fear stop them from acting.
